title: How to keep a site editable without a page-builder mess
excerpt: A custom website vs page builder choice is about what editors may change. Give them fields for those things. Keep the layout out of a free-form canvas.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The sketches fit a piece about structure that stays fixed while the words change.
caption: Editors change the content inside a structure, not the structure on a whim. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is a page builder the wrong tool?
faqs.answer: When the site has a design you want to keep, and the people editing it are not designers. A builder offers freedom on every pixel. Under a deadline that freedom becomes a new font, a new color, and a section that does not match the one above it. Structured fields avoid that mess by limiting the edit to the things that were meant to change.

faqs.question: Can a custom site still be editable?
faqs.answer: Yes. Put the headline, the body, the images, and the calls to action in fields an editor can change, with a preview on the real template. Leave navigation, type, and spacing in the design system. The editor publishes words and pictures, and does not rebuild the page.

faqs.question: What if we truly need a new layout often?
faqs.answer: Then budget for a person who designs, and give them a small set of sections they can reorder, not an infinite canvas. A handful of approved blocks keeps campaigns possible. An open builder makes every campaign a chance to abandon the brand. If every week needs a new design, that is a design practice, not a plugin.

markdown:
The custom website vs page builder decision is a decision about freedom. Editors need structured fields for the things that change: the headline, the paragraph, the image, the link. They do not need absolute freedom on every pixel. A builder sells that freedom as friendliness. On a site that just received a real design, the freedom is how the design comes apart.

A custom site can still be editable. The edit surface is simply smaller than the whole page. That limit is the product. It is how a founder changes the offer on a Thursday without also changing the type, the spacing, and the color of every button.

## What actually changes

List the changes from the last few months, or the changes you honestly expect. Wording on the homepage. A new project in the work grid. A post. A price, if you publish one. A photograph. Those are fields. They have labels. An editor can fill them without deciding where the button sits.

Everything else is design. The width of the column. The size of the headline. The color of the accent. The order of the navigation. Put those in the code and the design file, and change them when you mean to change the system. A builder that exposes them on every section will be used, because the control is there and the deadline is today. One reasonable tweak becomes the house style of whoever edited last.

Hanabi's marketing pages are built as a designed site, with editing reserved for the parts that are content. The articles live in Payload, with drafts, separate from the client portal. A post has a shape. It does not invite the writer to invent a new layout for the company in the middle of a paragraph. That is the trade in miniature. Voice and news can move. The page stays a page.

## What a builder is good at, and what it costs

A builder is good when the page is the experiment and the brand is not precious yet, or when a dedicated operator will police the canvas every week. It is good for a temporary campaign that will be deleted. It is a poor home for a company site that should still look like itself in a year.

The cost shows up as drift. Two heroes with two type scales. A section pasted from a template library. An image of the wrong crop. A button that says Click here because the field was free text and the person was in a hurry. None of these feel like a disaster on the day. Together they are a site nobody wants to send.

There is a second cost, in weight. Every widget, slider, and font the builder loads is a file your visitor waits on. [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) sets a plain bar: largest content within 2.5 seconds, the next paint after an interaction within 200 milliseconds, layout shift at 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile of loads. A custom page is not automatically inside those lines, and a builder page is not automatically outside them. Either one can be stuffed with decoration. The builder makes stuffing easier, because the decorations are checkboxes. If you use one, the same bar still applies. Freedom that costs the first view is too expensive.

## Fields, preview, and a short list of blocks

Give the editor a form, not a blank artboard. The homepage form might be a headline, a supporting sentence, one image, and one action. The work item might be a name, a summary, and a picture. The post might be a title, a body, and a date. Preview shows the real template, wrapping and all. Publish happens after the preview, not instead of it.

If the team truly campaigns, add a small set of blocks they may stack: a text section, a quote, an image, a call to action. They can reorder those. They cannot open a section and set an arbitrary font. The blocks were designed. The order is the freedom. This is enough range for a young company, and it is the range a small team can keep coherent.

Write the rules next to the fields, in one line. The headline is one sentence. The image is this crop. The button names the action. Google's questions about [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) belong in that margin. Does the heading describe the page, or does it exaggerate? Would a person who came directly to you learn what they needed? A builder will not ask. A field with a purpose makes the question harder to ignore, because the box is labeled with the job.

## How the mess starts, and how to refuse it

The mess starts with an exception. A launch partner wants a landing page that does not look like the site, and they want it tomorrow. Someone duplicates a template, restyles it, and publishes. The exception is now a second system. The next partner receives the second system because it is faster than the real one.

Refuse the exception in the tool, not only in a meeting. If the only way to publish is through the fields, the odd landing page has to be a real piece of work, designed and built, or it has to use the blocks. That friction is healthy. It keeps taste from being a race.

Review the live site monthly against the original page, not against your memory. Look for a color, a type size, and a button style that escaped. Put them back, and remove the control that let them escape if you can. A mess is easier to prevent than to clean, because cleaning requires someone to admit that a dozen small edits were wrong.

## A way to choose this month

If non-developers must edit every week, and the design should survive them, choose structured fields on a custom site. If a developer will make every change, and changes are rare, you may not need a CMS yet. The pages can live in the repository. If you need a page tomorrow and you have no design to protect, a builder is an honest temporary tool. Plan the exit. Temporary tools become the stack when nobody schedules the exit.

Ask one question of whatever you pick. Can a new teammate change the sentence without changing the brand? If the answer is yes, the tool fits. If the answer is that they can change anything, you have not given them an editor. You have given them the design job, unpaid, at the worst moment.

Who edits, and how often, is the question underneath the tool. [Choosing a CMS when the marketing team is small](/blog/choosing-a-cms) is the next piece. It stays with the editor, the rhythm, and the draft, before anyone argues about plugins.

When you want a site that is editable in the right places and strict everywhere else, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The build includes the fields. It does not include a canvas that will be regretted in a month.
